newsitem.title: CHILE: GOLD-Teck, Anglo revive Chile mine.
newsitem.headline: GOLD-Teck, Anglo revive Chile mine.

text.p: The $250 million deal between Canada's Teck Corp and Anglo American to build a gold mine at the Lobo-Marte deposits in northern Chile will be the South African mining giant's second stab at the Marte property.

This time the companies will build a traditional gold crushing mill, instead of using new, more risky heap-leaching technology which failed when Anglo American first developed the deposit in the late 1980s.
"A conventional gold mill costs a little more but it's a safer way to treat ores," Norman Keevil, Teck's president and CEO, told a news conference.
The new mine will use installations including a power plant and access road which were build for the first pit which shut down in 1991 after operating for just two years.
Gold production at the new project is expected to be between 275,000 and 350,000 ounces a year when the mine comes on line in around 2000.

The Marte property and the nearby Lobo site are owned by the newly formed company Minera Santa Rosa, which is 60-percent owned by Teck with 40 percent held by Anglo American units including Chile's Mantos Blancos.
Lying at a head-spinning 4,200 meters above sea level in the bleak Maricunga gold belt, the sites will be developed as separate open-cast mines with all ore crushed in a central mill.
This is the latest in a string of Canadian-owned mines to be developed in the belt which is home to Amax Gold's Refugio mine and Placer Dome's La Coipa pit.
Teck will arrange bank financing for between 50 and 60 percent of the project's costs which are expected to be around $200 million to $250 million, said Keevil.
The rest will be provided pro rata by the partners from their own resources, he said.
Teck Gold paid $51 million for its shareholding, including $35 million to Anglo American and $16 million to Cominco Resources COR.TO to buy its share in the Lobo deposit.
Although the mine has an initial working life of 10 years, this is likely to be extended as exploration reveals fresh mineral reserves, said Keevil.
"We want to extend the reserves with exploration during the feasibility study," he said.
"It's a large property with many areas worth looking at."
Teck, which owns 30 percent of the Quebrada Blanca copper mine in northern Chile, is investing around $12 million a year in exploration in Latin America, he said.
